findings.description: This bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration block, so objects are stored without a defined default encryption rule. It holds report data and a seeded vendor roster spreadsheet, so unencrypted storage exposes that data to anyone who obtains bucket-level or underlying storage access.

No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is associated with this bucket and no ACL is declared, so nothing prevents a later ACL or bucket policy from making the objects publicly readable. Defence in depth for S3 requires an explicit public access block.
The ledger export bucket defines no server_side_encryption_configuration, so financial ledger exports are stored without enforced default encryption (no SSE-KMS or SSE-S3 rule).
There is no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block guarding this bucket. The private ACL alone can be overridden by a future policy or ACL change, leaving sensitive financial exports exposed.

Versioning and access logging are enabled, but no server_side_encryption_configuration is set, so model artifacts (which frequently embed training data or proprietary logic) are stored without default encryption.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block resource is attached, so account- or bucket-level public access protections are not enforced for this bucket.

No server_side_encryption_configuration is defined. Operational runbooks commonly contain hostnames, escalation procedures, and credential-handling detail useful to an attacker, and they are stored unencrypted here.
This bucket has no associated aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, so it relies solely on the private ACL to remain non-public.

The audit log destination bucket has no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block. Because it is the target of access logging for other buckets, accidental exposure would reveal request metadata across the environment.

The acl value "lcatalogopts-delivery-write" is not a valid S3 canned ACL; the intended value is almost certainly "log-delivery-write". As written, the log delivery grant is not correctly applied, which can silently break audit log delivery and leave the environment without a usable audit trail.

force_destroy = true on the audit trail bucket allows Terraform to delete the bucket and all audit log objects without any protection, undermining the tamper-resistance expected of an audit log store. No object lock or MFA delete compensates for this.

The vendor-roster.xlsx object is uploaded with no server_side_encryption argument into aws_s3_bucket.reports_archive, which itself has no default encryption rule, so this file containing vendor/third-party data is written to S3 in an unencrypted state.

No logging block is configured for the bucket holding financial ledger exports, so there is no server-side record of who read or wrote objects, preventing detection or forensic reconstruction of data access.
No logging block is configured, so object-level access to the reports bucket is not recorded to the audit_trail bucket as it is for model_artifacts, leaving a gap in access accountability.
